764.title: The plague of Cyprian
764.hook: when plague came, letters from two bishops describe Christians staying to nurse the sick, their own and others
764.howItsDone: Christians count visiting the sick among the works of love in Matthew 25, and some churches organize hospital visits, meals and prayers for people who are ill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Origen reading: scripture built like a person, body, soul and spirit. Your line: read deeper.

"I was sick, and ye visited me." That's Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, describing the day the nations are gathered and sorted. The people who visited the sick are startled: when did we see you sick? And the answer: when you did it for the least of these, you did it for me. It's an easy line to admire on a calm day. It's a different line in a city where a disease is spreading, nobody knows how, and the sick are dying in their houses and streets. Two bishops, Cyprian in Carthage and Dionysius in Alexandria, lived through days like that, and their words survive.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Dionysius first. In a letter the historian Eusebius preserved, he describes what the Christians of Alexandria did in the plague, or most of them, he says. In paraphrase: out of great love, they didn't spare themselves. They clung to one another, visited the sick without fear and cared for them, and some who nursed others caught the disease and died, taking their neighbors' sickness on themselves. Others in the city, he says, pushed the sick away and fled, even from those dearest to them. That's one bishop's proud account of his own people. But the picture is specific: hands that wash and feed, and a cost that's paid. In Carthage, Cyprian's deacon Pontius wrote his bishop's life. When the plague came, he says, Cyprian taught his people that it isn't remarkable to care only for your own. If you want to be children of the Father, do good to everyone, even those who persecute you. Then he set them to work by what they had: the rich gave money, the poor their labor. Cyprian also wrote a short book, On Mortality, for frightened Christians who were dying too, and asking why. He doesn't pretend the plague spares them. He says it shows what's in people: whether the healthy care for the sick, whether families truly love each other, whether doctors stay with their patients. Not a statistic, and not a claim that only Christians were brave. Writing from two cities, saying one plain thing about their people. They stayed.
screen: `THE RICH GAVE MONEY, THE POOR LABOR.`

segments.voice: Let one face come: someone sick right now, in a hospital, in bed at home, or worn down by something long and quiet that others have stopped asking about. Think what would actually help, a message, soup, a ride, an hour of sitting with them; Cyprian's rule fits here: give what you have. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, hold them in mind.
Cyprian. The bishop of Carthage in whose days a plague struck, when writers in two cities said Christians nursed the sick, their own and others, even at the cost of their lives.
Your line: they stayed. Two cities, two bishops, and one plain thing to say. Be well.

765.title: Antony goes into the desert
765.hook: a young Egyptian hears 'go and sell that thou hast' read in church, and does it, and in time walks into the desert
765.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Antony as a father of monasticism and keep his feast; monks and nuns take vows of poverty, while other Christians practice the same verse through giving and simple living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyprian, and two cities where Christians nursed the sick through a plague. Your line: they stayed.

A young man in an Egyptian village has just buried his parents. He's inherited good farmland, and he's responsible for his little sister. Walking to church, he's turning something over: the apostles left everything to follow Jesus, and in the book of Acts, believers sold their land and laid the money at the apostles' feet. What would that look like now? He walks in, and at that moment the Gospel being read is the one about a rich young man. His name is Antony. His Life was written by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Here's the verse he heard, from Matthew, in the King James Bible: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me." Athanasius says Antony felt the words had been read for him. In the Gospel, the rich young man goes away sorrowful. Antony goes out and does it. He gives his family's land to the people of his village, sells the rest, and gives the money to the poor, keeping a little back for his sister. Then he walks into church again and hears another line: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow." So he gives away what he'd kept, places his sister with a community of faithful women, and begins a life of prayer and work. He doesn't vanish into the sand that afternoon. He starts at the edge of his village, learning from an old man who lives that way, moves out to the tombs, and only later crosses into the desert, farther and farther in. Athanasius says he wrote the Life because monks in other places asked what Antony was like. Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Antony as a father of monastic life, and there the call to sell everything is a real vocation some are given. Other Christians, among them some Protestants, read the verse as aimed at what holds a person's heart, and practice it through generosity rather than leaving home. Both readings take the verse seriously. What lands is the speed. He heard. And he went.
screen: `THE VILLAGE EDGE, THE TOMBS, THE DESERT.`
`A VOCATION, OR A MATTER OF THE HEART?`

segments.voice: Walk in your mind through a closet, a shelf or a drawer, and find one thing you don't need that someone else could use, not the easiest junk but something with a little weight to it. Decide where it would go; if you pray, offer it to God as you let it go, and if not, hold it in your mind and open your hand.
Antony. A young Egyptian who heard go and sell that thou hast, gave it away, and step by step walked into a life of prayer in the desert.
Your line: he heard, and went. No waiting to feel ready. Day seven hundred sixty-five, done.

766.title: Constantine
766.hook: an emperor sees a sign before battle, and everything changes for the church, for good and ill
766.howItsDone: The Orthodox Church honors Constantine as a saint, together with his mother Helena; other Christians remember him as a pivotal and debated figure in the church's history with the state.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antony, who heard go and sell that thou hast, and did it. Your line: he heard, and went.

For days now, the people in this story have been on the wrong side of power: a letter explaining Christians to outsiders, Justin writing to the emperor, Perpetua in the arena, Tertullian daring the governors, Cyprian's people nursing the sick. Today the camera turns around. A Roman ruler named Constantine is marching on Rome to fight a rival for the empire, and before the battle, by his own account, he sees something in the sky. He is not a Christian. He's about to become a very powerful friend to the church, and that changes the story.

Two old accounts survive, and they don't match exactly. Eusebius, a bishop who knew Constantine, writes that the emperor told him, and swore to it, that around noon he saw a cross of light above the sun, with words: by this, conquer. That night, Eusebius says, Christ appeared to him in a dream and told him to copy the sign and carry it into battle. So Constantine had a standard made with the first two Greek letters of Christ's name. Lactantius, another writer of the time, tells it more simply: in a dream, Constantine was told to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers' shields, and he did. A vision, a dream, or both; the sources differ. What happened next: Constantine won, and he favored the church. Christians who had been hunted found their emperor on their side. Their buildings could rise in public. Their bishops could meet openly. And the other side: when the emperor is your friend, the emperor has opinions about your church. Faith and power start to tangle in ways Christians have argued about since. Jesus had said, "My kingdom is not of this world." Now a kingdom of this world carried his sign into battle. Christians still weigh this differently. Some see Constantine as God's answer to the prayers of the persecuted, and the Orthodox Church honors him as a saint. Others see the moment the church began to trade the arena for the palace, and wonder what it cost. Some hold both. One more detail from Eusebius: Constantine was baptized only near the end of his life.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where you hold a little power: at work, at home, in a group, over someone newer than you. Ask what your beliefs, about God or about people, ask of you there, and where the power might be shaping the belief. If you pray, bring that place before God; if not, look at it honestly for this minute.
Constantine. The emperor who said he saw a sign before battle, and who turned the church from hunted to favored, for good and ill.
Your line: power changes things. For good, and for ill, and Christians still argue which. See you tomorrow.

767.title: The Edict of Milan (313)
767.hook: Christianity becomes legal, and the persecuted become the favored
767.howItsDone: Some churches pray in their services for those in authority and for people who suffer for their faith, and some Christian groups work for religious freedom for people of every faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantine: a sign before battle, and a church turned from hunted to favored. Your line: power changes things.

A notice goes up on a public wall in Nicomedia, a great city of the eastern empire. It's a letter from two emperors who have met at Milan and agreed on how the empire will treat religion: Constantine, who ruled the west, and Licinius, who was taking hold of the east. The writer Lactantius copied it out in full, and noted where it was posted: the same city where, by his account, an order to tear down churches and burn scriptures had been nailed up some years before. Same city, opposite message. People who had hidden their books, buried their friends and kept their heads down could walk past and read it.
screen: `A NOTICE ON A WALL IN NICOMEDIA.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the emperors grant to Christians, and to all others, the free power to follow whatever religion each person chooses. Not Christians instead of everyone else: Christians and everyone else. The reason sounds very Roman: so that whatever divine power there is in heaven may be kindly toward us and toward all who live under our rule. Then it gets practical. Meeting places and property taken from Christians are to be handed back at once, without payment, and anyone who bought one in good faith can ask the state for compensation. Freedom isn't only a sentence; it's a key returned to a door. Now the name. What we call the Edict of Milan reaches us as a letter, the copy Licinius had posted in Nicomedia. The name stuck anyway. Then the turn: the persecuted become the favored. Eusebius keeps letters from the months that follow in which Constantine sends money to clergy in Africa and frees clergy from public duties. The first letter to Timothy had asked prayers "for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life." Here was that quiet life, arriving all at once. And for good and ill: the letter's words were freedom for all. Some readers point out that later, when Christians held power, that promise didn't always hold for others. The long story has both.
screen: `AN EDICT THAT REACHES US AS A LETTER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person near you whose faith is different from yours, or who has none, and picture them on an ordinary day keeping what they keep: a prayer, a fast, a holiday, a quiet Sunday morning with no church in it. Don't argue with it; just let them be free in the picture. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, simply wish them well, as they are.
Constantine. One of the two emperors whose agreement at Milan gave Christians, and all others, freedom to follow their own religion, and handed back what had been taken.
Your line: freedom for all. Christians, and all others, in one breath. That's day seven hundred sixty-seven.

768.title: Nicaea (325)
768.hook: bishops gather over Arius' teaching and write: of one substance with the Father
768.howItsDone: Christians in Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches say the Nicene Creed together in worship, standing, often on Sundays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter from Milan: freedom for Christians and all others. Your line: freedom for all.

One Greek word: homoousios. Bishops traveled across the empire to argue over it, emperors took sides, and people were sent into exile for saying it or for refusing to. Here's why. In Alexandria, a priest named Arius was teaching that the Son of God was the first and greatest thing God made. Glorious, above everything else, but made: not God in the same way the Father is God. His bishop objected. The argument spread, and the emperor Constantine called bishops together at a city called Nicaea to settle it.

Arius wasn't a careless thinker. He was protecting something: God is one, and nothing can share God's being. So the Son, he reasoned, must be something God made. The creed that came out of Nicaea ended by rejecting a saying of his side, that there was a time when the Son was not. The bishops, Athanasius later wrote, searched the Bible for words to answer him, and kept finding that Arius could agree with them. The Son is from God? Yes, he'd say, so is everything. So they reached for a word that isn't in the Bible at all. Homoousios: of the same being, of one substance. The Son isn't like the Father in a high and noble way. He is what the Father is. A word from outside scripture, chosen to protect what they believed scripture already said. John's Gospel opens, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." And Jesus says in John, "I and my Father are one." The bishops heard those lines as more than closeness. The creed later prayed in churches is a fuller form, which we'll meet later on this path. In the old English of the Book of Common Prayer, its lines on the Son run: "Very God of very God, Begotten, not made, Being of one substance with the Father." Very, there, means true. Begotten, not made: a son, not a product. Why does it matter? Christians who say this creed are saying that when they look at Jesus, they aren't looking at God's best creation. They're looking at God.
screen: `ARIUS: THERE WAS WHEN HE WAS NOT.`

segments.voice: If the Nicene Creed is part of your tradition, say it slowly now and stop on the lines about the Son. If it isn't, let four phrases go by, one per breath: God of God, light of light, very God of very God, begotten, not made. Don't try to solve them; just notice which one catches.
Homoousios. Greek for of the same being, of one substance. The word the bishops at Nicaea chose to say the Son is what the Father is, not something the Father made.
Your line: true god from true god. One word, guarding a whole belief. Until tomorrow.

769.title: Athanasius against the world
769.hook: exiled again and again, he held to Nicaea when it was unpopular
769.howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and other churches honor Athanasius as a saint and teacher of the faith, and his On the Incarnation is still read in churches and classrooms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, homoousios: of one substance, the Son is what the Father is. Your line: true god from true god.

Winning the vote isn't the end of an argument. Nicaea chose its word, and the argument kept going. Bishops who'd signed changed their minds. Emperors came and went, and some leaned toward Arius' side. And one stubborn bishop of Alexandria, Athanasius, would not let the word go. He was sent away from his city and came back, sent away again and came back again. He hid. He wrote. He was accused of crimes, and answered the charges in writing. Later generations gave him a short Latin nickname: Athanasius contra mundum. Athanasius against the world. It didn't look like a hero on a hill. It looked like a man packing a bag, again.

What was he holding on to? In his book On the Incarnation, he gives the reason in one swing of a sentence. In paraphrase: God became human, so that humans might become divine. Only God can bring people home to God, he argued. If the Son is a creature, however grand, the bridge doesn't reach. So homoousios wasn't a word game. It was the whole rescue. Now the exiles. He's sent as far as Trier, in Gaul, a long way from the Nile. Other times he disappears into Egypt, sheltered, the stories say, by the desert monks. He later wrote the Life of Antony, the man who heard a Gospel line read in church and went into the desert. Here's a surprise. When enemies mocked him for running instead of staying to die, he wrote a defense of his flight. Jesus himself withdrew when they sought to kill him, he pointed out. And Paul escaped Damascus this way: "through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands." Standing firm, for Athanasius, didn't mean standing still for the soldiers. It meant not changing the word. Run if you must, hide if you must, but don't sign what you believe is false. Was he easy to deal with? His opponents brought real charges against him, which he denied, and he could be a hard man to cross. But the nickname stuck because, for long stretches, he seemed nearly alone, and he didn't move.
screen: `GOD BECAME HUMAN, SO HUMANS MIGHT RISE.`

770.title: Nicholas of Myra
770.hook: a bishop who, the story goes, dropped gold through a poor family's window by night
770.howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians keep a feast of Saint Nicholas, and in some countries children find small gifts in their shoes or stockings that morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Athanasius, who ran and hid but wouldn't change the word. Your line: against the world.

A bag lands on the floor in the dark. It came through the window, and inside there's gold. A bishop named Nicholas, in Myra, a town near the southern coast of what's now Turkey. The red coat, the sleigh and the reindeer come much later, and from somewhere else. Before any of that, there's a family in trouble, a window, and a man who very much didn't want to be thanked. We know little about Nicholas from records of his own time. Mostly we have the story people told about him, and the way his church remembered him.

The old Lives of Nicholas tell it this way. A man in Nicholas's town had been well off and lost everything. He had three daughters, and no money for their dowries, which meant no marriages. The story says he was close to a terrible choice: letting his daughters be sold into shame to keep the household alive. Nicholas heard. He didn't knock, call a meeting or make a speech. At night he threw a bag of gold through the window, and left. The father found it and wept, and the first daughter was married. Nicholas came back another night and did it again. On the third night, the father was waiting. He ran after the shadow in the street, caught up, and fell at his feet. And Nicholas begs him to tell no one. That's the center of the story: not the gold, the secret. It sounds like Jesus in Matthew's Gospel: "when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret." As the story tells it, Nicholas didn't want the father to owe him, or feel watched, or have to be grateful in public. He wanted three young women safe and a father to keep his dignity. Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor him as a saint, and in some places children still find gifts on his feast. Whatever the history behind it, the story keeps one shape: help that arrives in the dark, with no name on it.

Let one person come who could use help and wouldn't like to ask: a neighbor, a relative quietly having a hard month. Think of one gift you could give without your name on it, groceries left on a step, a good word said about them when they're not there, and picture yourself walking away before anyone sees. If you pray, pray for them.
Nicholas. A bishop near the southern coast of what's now Turkey who, the story goes, threw gold through a poor family's window by night, and begged not to be thanked.
Your line: a gift by night. A plague, a desert, an emperor, a letter, a word, an exile and a window: that was the week. Rest well.
